A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): whorled (multiple leaves are clearly attached at the same node, visible in close-up images; at least 5 leaves radiating from a single node)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): clustered (leaves are grouped tightly at the apex of the stem, forming a rosette-like cluster)

B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): simple (each leaf is a single, undivided blade)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): N/A (leaf complexity is simple)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): N/A (leaf complexity is simple)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): N/A (leaf complexity is simple)

C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth and unbroken, despite some damage; no natural teeth or serrations observed)

    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tip is sharply pointed)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): rounded (base is gently curved, not tapered or heart-shaped)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (main vein runs from base to apex, with lateral veins branching off and running to margin)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, closely spaced, numerous (secondary veins are clearly visible, forming a dense network; spacing is tight, with many veins per leaf)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (surface has a glossy appearance, reflecting light; some areas appear dull due to damage or debris)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or fuzz on leaf surface; surface appears smooth)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petiole is relatively short, not extending far from the stem to leaf base)

    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): woody (stem is firm, dark, and appears lignified; consistent with young tree seedling)

rag_matches.description: Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Functionally unisexual tree, to 18 m tall, to 27 cm dbh; outer bark thin, flaking in firm sheets, lenticellate; inner bark moderately thick, reddish; sap slowly forming viscid, cloudy droplets after slash, with strong, sweet aroma; stems glabrous, prominently brown-lenticellate. Leaves imparipinnate; petioles flattened above with sharp margins; petiolules thickened at both ends; leaflets 5-9 (13), mostly oblong to oblong-elliptic, acuminate with blunt acumen, acute to rounded at base, often ± inequilateral, 10-20(27) cm long, 5-9(12) cm wide, glabrous except for minute papillae. Panicles axillary, near stem apex, the branches ferruginous; staminate inflorescences somewhat larger than pistillate inflorescences (to 24 cm long); flowers 5-parted, sessile, 3.5-5 mm long; calyx to 2 mm long, cupulate, 5-lobed, minutely pubescent, the lobes acute; petals lanceolate, yellow-green, thickened medially on outside, ca 3 mm long, erect to somewhat spreading at anthesis; stamens 10, alternately long and short, the longest to 2 mm long, the shortest to 1.3 mm long, scarcely longer than the prominent, pubescent disk; ovary ovoid, densely pubescent; style short, the ovary and style together ca 2.7 mm long; stigma 5-lobed, persisting in fruit. Capsules drupaceous, bearing 1-5 pyrenes, ovoid to depressed-globose, with 4 or 5 lobes (rarely 2- or 3-lobed), mostly 2-3 cm diam, red at maturity, usually rounded at both ends, the carpels 4 or 5, each dehiscing by a single valve, the valve falling free to expose the white mesocarp surrounding the pyrene; pyrenes black, 1 per carpel, 1-seeded, ovoid in face view, irregular in side view. Croat 11109, 14822. Common along the shore; occasional in the forest. Flowers chiefly in April and May. The fruits mature chiefly in the middle of the rainy season (August to October). Small bees, possibly Trigona species, have been seen visiting the flowers. The fruits are edible. Costa Rica and Panama. In Panama, known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Chiriqui Province, Panama, and Darien Province. Reported from tropical wet forest in Costa Rica (Holdridge et al, 1971).

St.-Hil. By C.C. Berg. Shrubs or trees, dioecious. Leaves alternate and distichous; blade subcoriaceous to coriaceous, margins entire to serrated, pinnate-veined; lateral stipules, free. Inflorescences in the axils of the leaves or just below the leaves, racemose to spike-like, pedunculate, bracted. Staminate flowers: tepals 4, basally connate; stamens 4, straight or slightly bent at the tip; pistillode absent. Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

3. Terminalia L., nom. cons. Buceras P. Browne, Bucida L. by C.A. Stace. Trees or shrubs, sometimes spiny. Leaves alternate or spirally arranged, without glandular trichomes. Inflorescences simple, expanded or rarely in condensed axillary spikes. Flowers bisexual or bisexual and staminate in the same inflorescence, actinomorphic; upper part of the hypanthium funnel-shaped to bell-shaped; sepals 5, somewhat short to very short; petals absent; stamens 10, exserted, anthers versatile; style free. Dry fruit, with (1-)2-5(-6) wings, either dry or succulent and ribbed to terete, sometimes with the upper part of the hypanthium and the calyx persistent on it. 150-200 spp. Pantropical, with 33 spp. in America, from the United States and Mexico to Argentina. Leaves distichous; blade generally serrated, sometimes entire. Inflorescences solitary or paired, spicate or racemose (in Costa Rica), shortly pedunculated. Flowers sessile or pedicellate, the staminate with the perianth 4-parted, the segments imbricate; stamens 4, the filament straight in the bud; pistillate flowers with the perianth tubular, subentire or 4-lobed; ovary free or adnate to the perianth at the base; style 1 with 2 short stigmatic arms. Fruits drupaceous, completely immersed in the growing fleshy perianth. Vegetatively, Sorocea could be confused with Trophis and even with Batocarpus. From the former genus, Trophis, it differs in that Trophis has long and slender stigmas, while Sorocea has short and thick ones; Batocarpus differs by having syncarpous infructescences.

Guavita cansa-boca, Bribri, Guava, Guava del mono Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. The fruits mature within 1 month. Costa Rica to Peru and Brazil. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Colon and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone (Pipeline Road), Veraguas, and Panama (Cerro Jefe). [Paullinia turbacensis] is a tendriled liana; stems terete, ± glabrous, bearing conspicuous brown lenticels; sap at periphery milky, not copious. Leaves trifoliolate; petioles to 14 cm long, with marginal ribs above, glabrate; leaflets broadly elliptic, acuminate or acute at apex, attenuate to rounded at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-12 cm wide (to 23 cm long and 11 cm wide as juveniles), glabrate but with axillary tufts below, subentire to remotely crenate-dentate. Thyrses small, helicoid, to 7 cm long, solitary or clustered at nodes, often on leafless stems near the ground but occurring to 5 m high; flowers white, ca 5 mm long; petals with the scales ca two-thirds as long as petals, yellow-crested, the anterior scales bilobed, their appendages pubescent, the glands white, acute, densely pubescent; staminal cluster equaling petals; filaments densely pubescent; nectar abundant, stored near the large glands; ovary glabrous; styles pubescent. Capsules elliptic to obovate, 2 cm long, red, short-pubescent, the 3 boat-shaped valves broadly spreading to expose seeds; seeds 1-3, black, shiny, less than 1 cm long, covered on the lower half by a fleshy white aril, dangling on a thin funiculus when fully displayed.

Leaves alternate and distichous; blade leathery to chartaceous, entire, pinnate-veined; stipules completely amplexicaul and connate or semi-amplexicaul and free. Inflorescences in the axils of the leaves, bisexual or unisexual, pedunculate; receptacle globose, hemispherical, turbinate or convexly discoid, initially completely covered by peltate bracts. Staminate flowers several to numerous; perianth well developed, vestigial or absent; stamens 1-4; pistillode absent. Pistillate flowers 1-several, embedded in the receptacle; ovary adnate to the perianth; stigmas 2, filiform to vine-like. Fruits forming a drupe along with the enlarged, fleshy, and often colored receptacle. Seed large, without endosperm; cotyledons thick, equal or unequal. Approx. 15 spp. Tropical America.
